The capital of Kazakhstan is **Astana**. You're right that it has changed names several times: it has had about five names since the 1800s, and it has been called Astana twice.

**Name history**

| Period | Name | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1830 (some sources say 1824) | **Akmola** / **Akmolinsk** | Founded as a Russian military outpost. It was renamed Akmolinsk when it became a town; sources give 1832 or 1862 for that. |
| 1961 | **Tselinograd** | Renamed during Khrushchev's Virgin Lands Campaign. The name means "City of the Virgin Lands." |
| Early 1990s (sources give 1991 or 1992) | **Akmola** | The Kazakh name came back after independence. |
| 10 Dec 1997 | (still Akmola) | Replaced **Almaty** as the national capital. |
| 6 May 1998 | **Astana** | The name means "capital city" in Kazakh. |
| 23 Mar 2019 | **Nur-Sultan** | Named after Nursultan Nazarbayev, the long-time president, right after he resigned. |
| 17 Sep 2022 | **Astana** again | President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a constitutional amendment bringing back the name Astana. |

People sometimes think Almaty is still the capital. It's the country's largest city and its business center, but it hasn't been the capital since 1997.

**Abuja is the capital of Nigeria.** Lagos used to be the capital. The government officially moved to Abuja in December 1991 (most sources say 12 December). Many people still think Lagos is the capital because it is much bigger and better known.

**Why the capital moved**
- **Overcrowding:** Lagos had grown so fast that it was crowded and short on space. It is a coastal city of lagoons and islands, so it can't easily expand.
- **Central location and national unity:** Lagos is in the far southwest, in the Yoruba heartland. Abuja sits near the middle of the country, on land not dominated by any one of Nigeria's big ethnic groups. Some historians also say northern political leaders wanted the capital closer to their base.
- **It was controversial:** Obafemi Awolowo, a leading Yoruba politician, led the main opposition to the move. Local people were also moved off the land to make room for the new city.
- **It was gradual:** Abuja was built from scratch as a planned city. The decision came in the 1970s, but the official move didn't happen until 1991, and some government offices stayed in Lagos for years afterward.

**How they differ**

| | **Abuja** | **Lagos** |
|---|---|---|
| Role | Political capital: presidency (Aso Rock), National Assembly, Supreme Court, embassies | Economic and commercial hub: most banks and big companies have their headquarters here, plus the main port and a big tech scene |
| Origin | Purpose-built planned city | Old port city that grew over centuries |
| Size | Much smaller (a few million in the wider area) | One of Africa's largest cities. Estimates vary a lot, from about 16 million to more than 26 million, with about 30 million in the metro area |
| Administration | Federal Capital Territory (FCT), run by the federal government and not part of any state | Lagos State, one of Nigeria's 36 states |
| Location | Centre of the country, inland, hilly | Southwest coast, on lagoons and islands |
| Feel | Wide roads, more orderly, quieter, more expensive housing | Busy and fast-paced, famous for traffic jams (locally called "go-slows"), and the centre of music (Afrobeats), Nollywood films, nightlife and beaches |

**In short:** Abuja is where the government is, and Lagos is where most of the money, business and culture are. It's a bit like Canberra and Sydney, or Brasília and São Paulo.

**At noon in Kathmandu, it's 11:45 a.m. in Delhi.** Nepal is 15 minutes ahead of India. Nepal uses UTC+5:45 and India uses UTC+5:30. Neither country changes its clocks for daylight saving, so the 15-minute gap stays the same all year.

**Why Nepal uses an unusual offset**

- **It follows Nepal's own sun.** Most countries set their clocks to a whole or half hour from UTC. Nepal set its standard time by a meridian that runs through the peak of Gauri Shankar, a mountain about 100 km east of Kathmandu. That longitude works out to roughly UTC+5:45. Kathmandu's true local solar time is about UTC+5:41, so 5:45 matches local daylight closely.
- **India's clock fits Nepal poorly.** Indian Standard Time is based on a longitude of 82.5°E, near Prayagraj (Allahabad), which is well west of most of Nepal. Using UTC+5:30 would leave Nepal's clocks a bit behind its actual daylight.
- **The history:** Until 1920, Nepal used local solar time (Kathmandu mean time, about UTC+5:41:16). From 1920 it used Indian Standard Time (UTC+5:30). On 1 January 1986, Nepal moved its clocks forward 15 minutes and created Nepal Standard Time at UTC+5:45.
- **National identity is a possible extra reason.** Many people say the change also helped Nepal show it was separate from India. That is believable for a small country between India and China, but I couldn't find an official source for it. The geographic reason above is the documented one.

**Other unusual offsets:** Nepal is one of very few places at :45. The others are New Zealand's Chatham Islands (UTC+12:45, or +13:45 in summer) and an unofficial zone in a small area of Western Australia (UTC+8:45). India's own half-hour offset is also less common than whole hours.

Bhutan is a small, landlocked Buddhist kingdom in the Eastern Himalayas, between China (Tibet) to the north and India to the south. It's known for measuring progress by "Gross National Happiness," for its well-preserved culture and forests, and for a high-value, low-volume approach to tourism.

## Quick facts (as of October 2026)
- **Capital and largest city:** Thimphu
- **Area:** about 38,400 km² (14,800 sq mi), roughly the size of Switzerland. Almost all of it is mountainous, with subtropical plains along the southern border.
- **Population:** about 727,000 in the 2022 census. Other estimates range up to about 800,000.
- **Government:** a constitutional monarchy with a two-chamber parliament (National Assembly and National Council).
  - **King:** Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck, the fifth "Dragon King," crowned in 2008.
  - **Prime Minister:** Tshering Tobgay
- **Official language:** Dzongkha. English is widely used in schools and government.
- **Religion:** about 75% Vajrayana Buddhism (the state religion), about 23% Hindu (mostly in the south), and a small Bön minority.
- **Currency:** the ngultrum (BTN), pegged one-to-one with the Indian rupee.
- **Highest peak:** Gangkhar Puensum, about 7,570 m. It's often called the highest unclimbed mountain in the world, partly because Bhutan banned climbing its high peaks out of respect for local beliefs.

## History in brief
- **1600s:** Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, a Tibetan lama, unified the valleys into one state. He fought off Tibetan invasions, created a legal code and built the network of *dzongs* (fortress-monasteries) that still house both government offices and monks.
- **1907:** Ugyen Wangchuck was chosen as hereditary king, which started the Wangchuck dynasty. Britain, and later India, had influence over Bhutan's foreign affairs through treaties signed in 1910 and 1949. That arrangement was revised in 2007 and finally ended in 2011.
- **2008:** The monarchy itself pushed the country toward democracy. Bhutan adopted a written constitution and held its first parliamentary elections, becoming a constitutional monarchy.
- **A darker chapter:** In the late 1980s and early 1990s, citizenship and census rules targeted the Lhotshampa, people of Nepali descent living in the south. Tens of thousands were expelled or fled, with estimates up to about 100,000, and many spent years in refugee camps in Nepal. Since 2008 most have been resettled in Western countries, including the US.

## Gross National Happiness (GNH)
The fourth king coined the idea that "Gross National Happiness is more important than Gross Domestic Product." Policy is meant to balance economic growth with wellbeing, culture, good governance and the environment. In practice it's debated. The GNH Commission was dissolved in 2022, and the country struggles with youth unemployment and many young Bhutanese emigrating, especially to Australia.

## Environment
Bhutan is famous for being carbon-negative: its forests absorb more CO₂ than the country emits. The constitution requires at least 60% of the land to stay forested. The economy depends heavily on hydropower, much of which is sold to India. Wildlife includes takins (the national animal), snow leopards, red pandas, tigers and black-necked cranes.

## Economy and new projects
Hydropower, agriculture and tourism are the main sources of income. The biggest new initiative is **Gelephu Mindfulness City**, announced in December 2023. It's a large special economic zone on the southern border with India, meant to become a "mindful" business and financial hub, loosely modeled on places like Singapore and Dubai.

## Culture
- **Dress:** Citizens wear national dress, the *gho* for men and the *kira* for women, in schools, government offices and dzongs.
- **Architecture:** There are building codes that keep traditional styles.
- **Festivals:** *Tshechu* festivals feature masked dances held in monastery courtyards. Paro and Thimphu tshechus are the best known.
- **Archery** is the national sport.
- **Food:** The national dish is *ema datshi*, chillies cooked in cheese. Red rice and butter tea are staples.
- **Other quirks:** Selling tobacco has long been heavily restricted. Bhutan only allowed television and the internet in 1999. Thimphu is often said to be the only capital with no traffic lights.

## Visiting (as of October 2026)
- **Policy:** Bhutan's tourism policy is "high value, low volume."
- **Sustainable Development Fee (SDF):** Most foreign visitors pay **US$100 per person per night**, half the original US$200. The reduced rate currently runs to **31 August 2027**. There's been no official word yet on what happens after that date.
  - Children under 6 pay nothing, and ages 6–11 pay half.
  - Indian nationals pay a much lower fee, about ₹1,200 per night.
- **Visa:** a one-time US$40 visa fee, applied for in advance. Indian, Bangladeshi and Maldivian nationals don't need a visa.
- **Rules may change:** Rules and fees are revised from time to time, so check the official Bhutan tourism site (bhutan.travel) or a licensed Bhutanese tour operator before booking.
- **Getting there:** Paro is the only international airport. Its approach through a narrow valley is famously tricky, and only specially certified pilots fly it. Druk Air and Bhutan Airlines connect it to cities such as Delhi, Kathmandu, Bangkok and Singapore. You can also enter overland from India, for example at Phuentsholing.
- **Highlights:**
  - Tiger's Nest (Paro Taktsang), the monastery on a cliff above the Paro valley
  - Punakha Dzong, where two rivers meet
  - Dochula Pass, with its 108 chortens and Himalayan views
  - Bumthang, the spiritual heartland
  - Phobjikha valley, where black-necked cranes spend the winter
  - Treks such as the Druk Path and the very demanding Snowman Trek
- **Best times:** spring (March–May) for rhododendrons, and autumn (September–November) for clear mountain views and big festivals. Since it's now late October, you're in peak season.

Bhutan is a small, landlocked Buddhist kingdom in the Eastern Himalayas, between China (Tibet) to the north and India to the south. It's known for measuring progress by "Gross National Happiness," for its well-preserved culture and forests, and for a high-value, low-volume approach to tourism.

## Quick facts (as of October 2026)
- **Capital and largest city:** Thimphu
- **Area:** about 38,400 km² (14,800 sq mi), roughly the size of Switzerland. Almost all of it is mountainous, with subtropical plains along the southern border.
- **Population:** about 727,000 in the 2022 census. Other estimates range up to about 800,000.
- **Government:** a constitutional monarchy with a two-chamber parliament (National Assembly and National Council).
  - **King:** Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck, the fifth "Dragon King," crowned in 2008.
  - **Prime Minister:** Tshering Tobgay
- **Official language:** Dzongkha. English is widely used in schools and government.
- **Religion:** about 75% Vajrayana Buddhism (the state religion), about 23% Hindu (mostly in the south), and a small Bön minority.
- **Currency:** the ngultrum (BTN), pegged one-to-one with the Indian rupee.
- **Highest peak:** Gangkhar Puensum, about 7,570 m. It's often called the highest unclimbed mountain in the world, partly because Bhutan banned climbing its high peaks out of respect for local beliefs.

## History in brief
- **1600s:** Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, a Tibetan lama, unified the valleys into one state. He fought off Tibetan invasions, created a legal code and built the network of *dzongs* (fortress-monasteries) that still house both government offices and monks.
- **1907:** Ugyen Wangchuck was chosen as hereditary king, which started the Wangchuck dynasty. Britain, and later India, had influence over Bhutan's foreign affairs through treaties signed in 1910 and 1949. That arrangement was revised in 2007 and finally ended in 2011.
- **2008:** The monarchy itself pushed the country toward democracy. Bhutan adopted a written constitution and held its first parliamentary elections, becoming a constitutional monarchy.
- **A darker chapter:** In the late 1980s and early 1990s, citizenship and census rules targeted the Lhotshampa, people of Nepali descent living in the south. Tens of thousands were expelled or fled, with estimates up to about 100,000, and many spent years in refugee camps in Nepal. Since 2008 most have been resettled in Western countries, including the US.

## Gross National Happiness (GNH)
The fourth king coined the idea that "Gross National Happiness is more important than Gross Domestic Product." Policy is meant to balance economic growth with wellbeing, culture, good governance and the environment. In practice it's debated. The GNH Commission was dissolved in 2022, and the country struggles with youth unemployment and many young Bhutanese emigrating, especially to Australia.

## Environment
Bhutan is famous for being carbon-negative: its forests absorb more CO₂ than the country emits. The constitution requires at least 60% of the land to stay forested. The economy depends heavily on hydropower, much of which is sold to India. Wildlife includes takins (the national animal), snow leopards, red pandas, tigers and black-necked cranes.

## Economy and new projects
Hydropower, agriculture and tourism are the main sources of income. The biggest new initiative is **Gelephu Mindfulness City**, announced in December 2023. It's a large special economic zone on the southern border with India, meant to become a "mindful" business and financial hub, loosely modeled on places like Singapore and Dubai.

## Culture
- **Dress:** Citizens wear national dress, the *gho* for men and the *kira* for women, in schools, government offices and dzongs.
- **Architecture:** There are building codes that keep traditional styles.
- **Festivals:** *Tshechu* festivals feature masked dances held in monastery courtyards. Paro and Thimphu tshechus are the best known.
- **Archery** is the national sport.
- **Food:** The national dish is *ema datshi*, chillies cooked in cheese. Red rice and butter tea are staples.
- **Other quirks:** Selling tobacco has long been heavily restricted. Bhutan only allowed television and the internet in 1999. Thimphu is often said to be the only capital with no traffic lights.

## Visiting (as of October 2026)
- **Policy:** Bhutan's tourism policy is "high value, low volume."
- **Sustainable Development Fee (SDF):** Most foreign visitors pay **US$100 per person per night**, half the original US$200. The reduced rate currently runs to **31 August 2027**. There's been no official word yet on what happens after that date.
  - Children under 6 pay nothing, and ages 6–11 pay half.
  - Indian nationals pay a much lower fee, about ₹1,200 per night.
- **Visa:** a one-time US$40 visa fee, applied for in advance. Indian, Bangladeshi and Maldivian nationals don't need a visa.
- **Rules may change:** Rules and fees are revised from time to time, so check the official Bhutan tourism site (bhutan.travel) or a licensed Bhutanese tour operator before booking.
- **Getting there:** Paro is the only international airport. Its approach through a narrow valley is famously tricky, and only specially certified pilots fly it. Druk Air and Bhutan Airlines connect it to cities such as Delhi, Kathmandu, Bangkok and Singapore. You can also enter overland from India, for example at Phuentsholing.
- **Highlights:**
  - Tiger's Nest (Paro Taktsang), the monastery on a cliff above the Paro valley
  - Punakha Dzong, where two rivers meet
  - Dochula Pass, with its 108 chortens and Himalayan views
  - Bumthang, the spiritual heartland
  - Phobjikha valley, where black-necked cranes spend the winter
  - Treks such as the Druk Path and the very demanding Snowman Trek
- **Best times:** spring (March–May) for rhododendrons, and autumn (September–November) for clear mountain views and big festivals. Since it's now late October, you're in peak season.

Here's a short briefing for a November trip. I've marked the figures that change over time.

## People
- **Population:** about 3.3 million at the 2020 census, and probably around 3.5 million now. That spread over a country roughly three times the size of France makes Mongolia the least densely populated sovereign state.
- **Ulaanbaatar:** about half the country lives in the capital (around 1.8 million people in 2025). Outside it, semi-nomadic herding is still the main way of life.
- **Ethnicity:** about 95.6% Mongol, mostly Khalkha (about 84% of the population). Kazakhs make up 3.8% and live mainly in the far west (Bayan-Ölgii).
- **Language:** Mongolian, written mainly in Cyrillic. The traditional vertical script is being revived in official use. Kazakh is spoken in the west. English is the most common foreign language among younger people in the city, and Russian among older people. Expect little English in the countryside.
- **Politics:** a parliamentary democracy. After a party power struggle and a constitutional crisis in late 2025, **Nyam-Osoryn Uchral** (Mongolian People's Party) became prime minister in late March 2026, replacing Gombojavyn Zandanshatar.

## Religion
- **2020 census:** Buddhist 51.7%, no religion 40.6%, Muslim 3.2% (mostly Kazakhs), shamanist 2.5%, Christian 1.3%.
- The Buddhism is **Tibetan Buddhism**. It was harshly suppressed under communism in the 1930s and has revived since 1990. Gandan Monastery in Ulaanbaatar is the main place to see it.
- Shamanist customs are common even among Buddhists, such as walking clockwise around *ovoo* (stone cairns) and leaving offerings at them. Follow what locals do, and don't step on the threshold of a ger (yurt).

## Economy
- **Mining runs the economy.** Most export income comes from coal and copper (the giant Oyu Tolgoi mine), plus gold. China buys most of the exports, which leaves the economy exposed to commodity prices and Chinese demand.
- **Growth:** 6.9% in 2025 (World Bank). For 2026 the World Bank forecasts about 5% and the EBRD 5.5%. The EBRD reports growth of 7.7% year on year in the first half of 2026, driven by coal and copper.
- **Herding** is the other pillar: tens of millions of sheep, goats, horses, cattle and camels, which is why cashmere is a major export and good to buy. Severe winters (*dzud*) can wipe out livestock.
- **Currency:** the tögrög (MNT). Cards work widely in Ulaanbaatar. Carry cash in the countryside.

## Weather in November
- **Very cold and dry.** Ulaanbaatar averages are about **−5 °C (23 °F) highs and −15 °C (5 °F) lows**, with a monthly mean of −10.6 °C. Nights can fall well below that; the record is −35 °C. The countryside, especially in the north and west, is often colder.
- **Little snow** (about 6 mm of precipitation, around 9 light-snow days) and **a lot of sun** (about 175 hours). Expect clear blue skies, biting wind, and short days.
- **Air pollution:** this is the main health issue. When the heating season starts, coal smoke, mostly from the ger districts, makes Ulaanbaatar one of the most polluted cities in the world, especially in the mornings and evenings. Bring N95/FFP2 masks, particularly if you have asthma or heart or lung problems.
- **What to pack:** thermal base layers, a down jacket, a windproof outer layer, an insulated hat, gloves (mittens are better), a face covering, warm insulated boots, lip balm and moisturiser (the air is extremely dry), and sunglasses. Phone batteries drain quickly in the cold, so keep your phone close to your body.
- November is off-season. You'll see few tourists and pay lower prices, but some ger camps close and countryside roads can be icy. Check that any tours are actually running.

The **lower 48 US states are bigger**, by roughly **390,000 km² (about 150,000 sq mi)**. That's about 5% more than Australia, or roughly the area of Germany or Montana.

| | Total area | |
|---|---|---|
| Contiguous US (48 states + D.C.) | ~8,080,000 km² | 3,119,885 sq mi |
| Australia (mainland + Tasmania + nearby islands) | ~7,688,000 km² | ~2,968,000 sq mi |
| **Difference** | **~392,000 km²** | **~151,000 sq mi** |

**How the measurements differ**
- **US figure:** The Census Bureau splits the lower 48 into about 2,959,064 sq mi of land and about 160,820 sq mi of water. The water figure includes the US share of the Great Lakes and some coastal and inland waters.
- **Australia figure:** Geoscience Australia's 7,688,287 km² is everything inside the coastline: 7,656,127 km² of mainland plus 32,160 km² of islands. It doesn't list inland water separately. Australia has very little permanent inland water anyway, and big salt lakes like Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre are usually dry and fall inside that figure.
- **Land only, it's close to a tie:** The lower 48's land area is about 7,664,000 km², which is slightly *smaller* than Australia's 7,688,000 km². So the US comes out ahead only once you count its water, mostly the Great Lakes.
- **Other figures you may see:** Some sources give Australia as about 7,741,000 km² because they add external territories such as Heard Island and Macquarie Island. Even then, the lower 48 is still about 340,000 km² larger. Older Australian yearbooks use 7,692,024 km², which also doesn't change the result.

**Bottom line:** Counting inland water, the contiguous US is about 5% larger than Australia. On land alone, the two are almost exactly the same size.

answer:
A Bloom filter is a compact way to test whether an item is in a set. A "no" answer is always right. A "yes" answer means "probably." It gets this trade-off because it only ever turns bits on and never turns them off.

## How it works

**The structure:** an array of *m* bits, all starting at 0, plus *k* different hash functions. Each hash function maps any item to one of the *m* positions.

**Adding an item:** run the item through all *k* hash functions to get *k* positions, and set each of those bits to 1. If a bit is already 1, it stays 1.

**Checking an item:** hash it the same way and look at its *k* bits.
- If **any** of them is 0, the item is **definitely not** in the set.
- If **all** of them are 1, the item is **probably** in the set.

The filter never stores the items themselves, only bits. That is why it's so small. At about 10 bits per item it gives roughly a 1% false-positive rate, whatever the size of the items.

### Small example
Use 10 bits and 3 hash functions.
- Add "cat": the hashes give positions 1, 4, 7, so those bits become 1.
- Add "dog": the hashes give positions 2, 4, 9, so those bits become 1.
- Bits now set: {1, 2, 4, 7, 9}.
- Check "cow" → 3, 4, 7. Bit 3 is 0, so "cow" is **definitely absent**.
- Check "eel" → 1, 2, 9. All three bits are 1, so the filter says **"probably present."** But "eel" was never added. Its bits were turned on by "cat" and "dog" together. That's a false positive.

## Why there are never false negatives

When an item is added, all *k* of its bits are set to 1. A standard Bloom filter has no way to set a bit back to 0. So any later check of that same item hashes to the same *k* bits, finds them all still 1, and answers "present." For the filter to say "absent," at least one of the item's bits would have to be 0, and that can't happen once the item has been added.

(This assumes a standard filter with deterministic hashes and no deletions. If you "delete" by clearing bits, you could clear a bit another item also uses and cause false negatives. Counting Bloom filters exist to handle deletion safely.)

## Why there can be false positives

Many items share the same bits. A "yes" only tells you that every one of the item's *k* bits was set by *something*, and that something may be a mix of other items. The filter has no record of who set which bit, so it can't tell a real member from a coincidental match. As more items are added, more bits become 1 and these collisions get more likely.

## How likely is a false positive?

With *m* bits, *k* hash functions and *n* inserted items, the standard approximation is:

**p ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k**

- After *n* insertions, any given bit is still 0 with probability about e^(−kn/m).
- A false positive needs all *k* probed bits to be 1, which gives the formula above.
- The best number of hash functions is **k ≈ (m/n)·ln 2**, which leaves about half the bits set.
- In practice: more bits per item means fewer false positives. Too few hash functions doesn't check enough bits, and too many fills the array too fast.

One caveat: this classic formula is an approximation. Researchers have shown it slightly *underestimates* the true rate, especially for small filters (Bose et al.; Christensen, Roginsky & Jimeno at NIST, 2010). For large filters it's accurate enough for normal engineering work.

## Where it's used

A Bloom filter is a compact way to test whether an item is in a set. A "no" answer is always right. A "yes" answer means "probably." It gets this trade-off because it only ever turns bits on and never turns them off.

## How it works

**The structure:** an array of *m* bits, all starting at 0, plus *k* different hash functions. Each hash function maps any item to one of the *m* positions.

**Adding an item:** run the item through all *k* hash functions to get *k* positions, and set each of those bits to 1. If a bit is already 1, it stays 1.

**Checking an item:** hash it the same way and look at its *k* bits.
- If **any** of them is 0, the item is **definitely not** in the set.
- If **all** of them are 1, the item is **probably** in the set.

The filter never stores the items themselves, only bits. That is why it's so small. At about 10 bits per item it gives roughly a 1% false-positive rate, whatever the size of the items.

### Small example
Use 10 bits and 3 hash functions.
- Add "cat": the hashes give positions 1, 4, 7, so those bits become 1.
- Add "dog": the hashes give positions 2, 4, 9, so those bits become 1.
- Bits now set: {1, 2, 4, 7, 9}.
- Check "cow" → 3, 4, 7. Bit 3 is 0, so "cow" is **definitely absent**.
- Check "eel" → 1, 2, 9. All three bits are 1, so the filter says **"probably present."** But "eel" was never added. Its bits were turned on by "cat" and "dog" together. That's a false positive.

## Why there are never false negatives

When an item is added, all *k* of its bits are set to 1. A standard Bloom filter has no way to set a bit back to 0. So any later check of that same item hashes to the same *k* bits, finds them all still 1, and answers "present." For the filter to say "absent," at least one of the item's bits would have to be 0, and that can't happen once the item has been added.

(This assumes a standard filter with deterministic hashes and no deletions. If you "delete" by clearing bits, you could clear a bit another item also uses and cause false negatives. Counting Bloom filters exist to handle deletion safely.)

## Why there can be false positives

Many items share the same bits. A "yes" only tells you that every one of the item's *k* bits was set by *something*, and that something may be a mix of other items. The filter has no record of who set which bit, so it can't tell a real member from a coincidental match. As more items are added, more bits become 1 and these collisions get more likely.

## How likely is a false positive?

With *m* bits, *k* hash functions and *n* inserted items, the standard approximation is:

**p ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k**

- After *n* insertions, any given bit is still 0 with probability about e^(−kn/m).
- A false positive needs all *k* probed bits to be 1, which gives the formula above.
- The best number of hash functions is **k ≈ (m/n)·ln 2**, which leaves about half the bits set.
- In practice: more bits per item means fewer false positives. Too few hash functions doesn't check enough bits, and too many fills the array too fast.

One caveat: this classic formula is an approximation. Researchers have shown it slightly *underestimates* the true rate, especially for small filters (Bose et al.; Christensen, Roginsky & Jimeno at NIST, 2010). For large filters it's accurate enough for normal engineering work.

## Where it's used

Bloom filters are useful when a fast, cheap "definitely not" lets you skip expensive work. Examples include databases such as Cassandra, HBase and RocksDB checking whether a key could be in a disk file before reading it, web caches, and spell-checkers. A false positive only costs an unnecessary lookup. A false negative would mean wrong results, and the design rules that out.

EIP-1559 replaced Ethereum's old blind-auction fee system with a **protocol-set base fee that is burned**, plus an **optional tip** that goes to whoever produces the block. It went live in the **London hard fork on August 5, 2021, at block 12,965,000**. It didn't make fees permanently cheap. What it did was make them **more predictable**, make blocks **flexible in size**, and **destroy part of every fee** instead of handing all of it to miners.

## Before EIP-1559: a first-price auction
- Each transaction had one `gasPrice`. Miners mostly picked the highest bids, and the miner received the **whole fee**.
- Users had to guess what to bid. When the network was busy, people overpaid to be safe, or underbid and had transactions stuck for hours.
- Every block had the same fixed gas limit, so a sudden jump in demand could only show up as a price spike.

## What EIP-1559 introduced

**1. Base fee (set by the protocol, then burned)**
- Every block has a per-gas `baseFee` that every transaction must pay. Users don't bid it. The protocol calculates it from how full the previous block was.
- The base fee is **burned**, meaning it's permanently removed from the ETH supply. Block producers don't get it.
- It started at 1 gwei at the fork block.

**2. Blocks that can grow and shrink, with a target size**
- Each block has a **gas target** equal to half its gas limit (the "elasticity multiplier" is 2). A block can use up to twice the target.
- If the previous block used more than the target, the base fee goes up. If it used less, the base fee goes down.
- The change is capped at **1/8 (12.5%) per block**. That makes the next base fee easy for wallets to predict, and a short burst of demand gets absorbed by bigger blocks before the price shoots up.
- Example: the original London parameters were a 15M target and 30M maximum. Validators can raise the gas limit without a hard fork, and they have. Ethereum.org's examples use a 36M limit (18M target), and validators pushed it to **60M in late 2025**. I didn't find a confirmed figure for October 2026, so it may have changed again.

**3. Priority fee (tip)**
- `maxPriorityFeePerGas` is a tip that goes to the block producer. Today that's the validator, since the Merge in 2022 replaced miners. The tip pays them to include your transaction and lets you outbid others when you're in a hurry.
- When the network isn't congested, a small tip is enough.

**4. Max fee and automatic refund**
- `maxFeePerGas` is the most you're willing to pay per gas in total. A transaction can only go into a block whose base fee is at or below this cap.
- You actually pay **base fee + tip**, capped at your max fee. Any difference is never charged, so setting a high cap to be safe doesn't cost extra.
- These fields come in a new **"type 2" transaction** format. Old-style transactions still work and are handled as if max fee and tip both equal their gas price.

## Worked example (from ethereum.org)
A simple ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas. With a 10 gwei base fee and a 2 gwei tip:
- Total: 21,000 × 12 gwei = 252,000 gwei (0.000252 ETH)
- Burned: 21,000 × 10 gwei = 0.00021 ETH
- To the validator: 21,000 × 2 gwei = 0.000042 ETH

## What changed in practice, and what didn't
- **Better user experience:** wallets can estimate fees reliably, there's less overpaying, and fewer transactions get stuck.
- **Supply and economics:** burning the base fee ties ETH's supply to network use. When activity is high, the amount burned can be larger than new ETH issued, so total supply shrinks. It also stops block producers from profiting by manipulating fees, since they don't receive the base fee.
- **Not a fix for high fees:** if demand stays high, the base fee keeps rising. Fees only come down by adding capacity, through higher gas limits and layer-2 rollups (helped by later upgrades like blobs in Dencun). EIP-1559 changed **how** fees are set and paid, not how much block space exists.

# NIST post-quantum signature algorithms, as of October 21, 2026

**In short:** NIST has published two final post-quantum signature standards, **ML-DSA (FIPS 204)** and **SLH-DSA (FIPS 205)**. A third one it has already chosen, **FN-DSA (Falcon, FIPS 206)**, is still a draft and not yet final. NIST has also approved two older stateful hash-based schemes, **LMS and XMSS**. Separately, it is still running a competition for more signature schemes, which has **nine candidates in Round 3**.

## 1. Final standards (published August 13, 2024)

| Standard | Algorithm (original name) | Math basis | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FIPS 204** | **ML-DSA** (CRYSTALS-Dilithium) | Lattices | Final. NIST's main recommended general-purpose PQ signature |
| **FIPS 205** | **SLH-DSA** (SPHINCS+) | Hash functions only (stateless) | Final. A conservative backup that doesn't rely on lattice math |

- **ML-DSA** is the default choice. Its keys and signatures are fairly small (a level-2 signature is about 2.4 KB) and it is fast. It is also the signature algorithm in NSA's CNSA 2.0 suite.
- **SLH-DSA** depends only on hash functions being secure, which is a well-understood assumption. The trade-off is large signatures (about 8–50 KB) and slow signing.
- **Update to FIPS 205:** On April 13, 2026, NIST released a draft, **SP 800-230**, called *Additional SLH-DSA Parameter Sets for Limited-Signature Use Cases*. It adds six parameter sets with smaller signatures and faster verification, meant for things like signing software, firmware and certificates. They only work safely if each key signs no more than **2^24 signatures** in its lifetime, and they are not approved for general use. Public comments closed June 12, 2026, and the document is not final yet.

## 2. Selected but not yet final: FN-DSA (Falcon), FIPS 206

- NIST picked Falcon in July 2022, along with Dilithium and SPHINCS+. It is lattice-based and has the most compact signatures of the three (about 666 bytes at level 1). The catch is that signing uses floating-point Gaussian sampling, which is hard to implement safely.
- NIST says the draft was submitted for internal approval in **August 2025**. At NIST's 6th PQC Standardization Conference (September 2025), Ray Perlner presented open design questions and asked for public input. These included separate "pure" and pre-hash versions, signing that is always randomized, a BUFF transform for stronger security properties, and possibly a fixed-point signing variant.
- **Current status:** I couldn't find a published Initial Public Draft of FIPS 206 on NIST's site. The expected draft page returns "not found", and an IETF draft from May 2026 still calls FIPS 206 "forthcoming". It looks like the public draft and comment period haven't happened yet, which means a final standard is unlikely before 2027. Industry estimates of "late 2026 to early 2027" are guesses, not NIST commitments.
- FN-DSA as standardized will **not be byte-for-byte compatible** with the original Falcon submission.

## 3. Stateful hash-based signatures (NIST SP 800-208, October 2020)

- **LMS/HSS** and **XMSS/XMSS^MT** are approved post-quantum signatures, but they are stateful. The signer must never reuse a one-time key, so tracking state carefully is essential. NIST recommends them mainly for narrow cases like firmware and code signing, not general use. CNSA 2.0 also allows LMS and XMSS for software and firmware signing.

## 4. Additional signatures competition (the "on-ramp")

NIST launched this in 2023 to find more signature schemes, especially ones not based on structured lattices and ones with short signatures. 40 schemes made Round 1 and 14 made Round 2 (October 2024). On **May 14, 2026**, NIST named **nine Round 3 candidates** and explained the choice in report **NIST IR 8610**:

- **Multivariate:** UOV, MAYO, QR-UOV, SNOVA
- **MPC-in-the-Head / VOLE-in-the-Head:** FAEST, MQOM, SDitH
- **Lattice:** HAWK (the only lattice scheme left)
- **Isogeny:** SQIsign (the only isogeny scheme; very small signatures, but slow)

Round 3 is expected to last **about two years**. The 7th PQC Standardization Conference is planned for late spring or early summer 2027. **None of these schemes is standardized yet.** Any that are selected would become standards only after that, likely late in this decade.

## Practical takeaway
- To deploy now, use **ML-DSA**. Use **SLH-DSA** if you want the most conservative security assumptions, and LMS/XMSS for firmware signing where you can manage state reliably.
- If signature size matters a lot, keep an eye on **FN-DSA**. Don't count on it being FIPS-validated until FIPS 206 is final.
- **HQC** (chosen in March 2025) is sometimes mentioned alongside these, but it is a key-encapsulation mechanism, not a signature scheme.

answer:
The short version: proof of stake (PoS) uses about 99.9%+ less energy than proof of work (PoW). On security, neither one simply wins. They are secure in different ways and have different weak spots. PoW is older and easier to reason about. PoS makes attacks cost the attacker their own stake, but its rules are more complex.

## How each one works

- **Proof of work (Bitcoin and others):** Miners compete to solve a puzzle by guessing over and over on special hardware. The winner adds the next block. Security comes from the fact that rewriting history means redoing all that computing work, which costs real hardware and electricity.
- **Proof of stake (Ethereum since 2022, and others):** Validators lock up the chain's coins as collateral. The protocol picks them to propose and vote on blocks. Security comes from the value of that collateral, which can be destroyed ("slashed") if a validator cheats.

## Energy

- **PoW uses a lot by design.** The energy spent is what makes attacks expensive. Estimates of Bitcoin's electricity use vary widely. Cambridge's live index was reported at about 138 TWh per year in mid-2026, within a possible range of about 74–242 TWh. Other estimates are higher: one report attributes about 190 TWh (December 2025) to Cambridge researchers, and Digiconomist puts it near 204 TWh. That's roughly what a mid-sized country uses. I only saw these figures through secondary sources, so treat the exact numbers as rough.
- **PoS uses very little.** Validators run on ordinary computers. When Ethereum switched from PoW to PoS on September 15, 2022 (the "Merge"), ethereum.org estimated its energy use fell by about 99.95%. Estimates put it at roughly 0.01 TWh per year afterward, down from tens of TWh before. The 99.95% figure is an estimate, not a measurement.
- **The other side of the argument:** Supporters of PoW say mining can use stranded or surplus energy and help balance power grids. Critics say that doesn't change the overall scale of use or emissions, which depend on where the electricity comes from.

## Security

| Aspect | Proof of work | Proof of stake |
|---|---|---|
| **What an attacker needs** | More than 50% of the mining power | 33% of stake to stop the chain from finalizing; more than 50% to control which chain wins; 66% or more to finalize a false history |
| **Cost of an attack** | Hardware plus ongoing electricity. The attacker keeps the hardware afterward and can attack again | Buying a huge amount of the coin, which drives its price up. Provable cheating gets the stake slashed, so the attacker loses it |
| **Recovering from an attack** | Hard. The honest side can only add more mining power or change the mining algorithm, which hurts honest miners too | The community can coordinate to leave the attacker's stake out of a recovery fork, so attackers can't just repeat the attack |
| **Finality** | Probabilistic. A payment becomes safer with each block on top (Bitcoin users often wait for about 6) | Ethereum has "economic finality" after about 2 epochs (about 13 minutes). Reversing a finalized block would cost at least ⅓ of all stake |
| **Track record and simplicity** | Bitcoin has run on it since 2009, and its rules are simple | Newer and more complex, which means more room for bugs. Ethereum PoS has run since 2022 without a successful consensus attack |
| **PoS-specific issues** | Doesn't apply | "Long-range" and "nothing-at-stake" attacks. These are handled with slashing and "weak subjectivity" checkpoints: a node that has been offline a long time needs a recent trusted checkpoint to rejoin |
| **Centralization risks** | Mining pools, cheap-power regions, and a few dominant hardware makers | Big staking providers and exchanges (for example Lido or Coinbase) holding large shares of stake, and wealth that compounds over time |

Some further points:

1. **Size matters more than the method.** A small PoW chain can be attacked by renting mining power. Ethereum Classic suffered several 51% attacks in 2020. A small PoS chain is also cheap to attack if its token is cheap. Big chains like Bitcoin and Ethereum are very expensive to attack under either system.
2. **Where the security lives.** PoW security rests on something outside the chain (energy and hardware). PoS security rests on the chain's own token. PoW fans say this makes PoW more objective. PoS fans say it lets the protocol punish attackers directly.
3. **Future funding.** Bitcoin's mining reward halves about every four years, so its long-term security budget depends more and more on transaction fees. This is an open debate.

## Bottom line

On energy, PoS wins clearly, by a factor of thousands. On security, both are considered strong for large networks. PoW offers simplicity, a long track record, and security tied to the physical world. PoS offers finality, the ability to punish attackers, and efficiency, but it's more complex and raises its own concerns about stake concentration. Which one you prefer depends on how you weigh those trade-offs.

answer:
**Short answer:** In a second-price (Vickrey) auction, bid exactly what the item is worth to you. In a first-price sealed-bid auction, bid less than your value ("shade" your bid). How much less depends mostly on how many people you're bidding against and how high you expect their values to be.

## Second-price (Vickrey): bid your true value

The highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid. So your bid decides **whether** you win. It does not decide **what you pay**. Bidding your true value v is a weakly dominant strategy (Vickrey, 1961). That means it is never worse than any other bid, whatever the others do:

- **Bidding above v** only changes the outcome when someone else's bid lands between v and your bid. Then you win and pay more than the item is worth to you, so you lose money.
- **Bidding below v** only changes the outcome when the top rival bid lands between your bid and v. Then you lose an item you could have bought at a profit.
- **Bidding exactly v** means you win whenever winning is profitable and lose whenever it isn't.

You don't need to guess anything about the other bidders. All the work is in figuring out your own value honestly.

## First-price sealed bid: shade your bid

The winner pays their own bid. If you bid your true value you make zero profit even when you win, so you have to bid below it. Lowering your bid has a tradeoff:

- You keep more profit when you win: v − b gets bigger.
- You win less often, because someone else is more likely to outbid you.

The best bid balances these two effects. In the standard textbook case (n bidders, risk-neutral, private values drawn independently and uniformly), the equilibrium bid is:

> **b(v) = ((n − 1)/n) × v**

| Bidders (n) | Bid as a share of your value |
|---|---|
| 2 | 50% |
| 3 | 67% |
| 5 | 80% |
| 10 | 90% |

A more general rule: bid what you expect the strongest rival's value to be, assuming yours is the highest. In symbols, b(v) = E[highest other value | it is below v]. In effect, you bid what you would have paid in a second-price auction.

**Example:** The item is worth $100 to you and you face one rival whose value is equally likely to be anywhere from $0 to $100. In a Vickrey auction, bid $100. In a first-price auction, bid about $50. With nine rivals, bid about $90.

## Practical rules for first-price bidding

1. **More competition means less shading.** As the number of bidders grows, bids move toward true values.
2. **Your beliefs about rivals matter.** If you expect strong rivals, shade less. If you expect weak ones, shade more. This is why first-price auctions reward research and strategy, and Vickrey auctions don't.
3. **Risk aversion means bidding higher.** If losing hurts more than overpaying a little, shade less. This matters in first-price auctions only. In a Vickrey auction the best bid is still your true value.
4. **Ties and bid levels:** Avoid round numbers. $50.37 beats someone else's $50.

## Two points that apply to both formats

- **Expected revenue is usually the same.** Under the standard assumptions, the seller expects the same revenue from either format (the revenue equivalence theorem). The lower first-price bids exactly offset the fact that Vickrey winners pay only the second-highest bid. With n uniform bidders, expected revenue is (n−1)/(n+1) in both cases.
- **Winner's curse with common values.** If the item has a shared value that everyone is estimating, such as an oil lease, you should lower your estimate in both formats. Winning means you were probably the most optimistic bidder. "Bid your value" in a Vickrey auction means your value given that you won, not your raw estimate.

## Where the theory breaks down

- **Trust in the seller:** Vickrey truthfulness assumes the seller won't add fake bids (shill bids) to push up the second price. That risk is one reason pure Vickrey auctions are rare in practice.
- **Real-world formats differ:** eBay's proxy bidding works roughly like a second-price auction, so entering your true maximum there is sensible. Many online ad exchanges switched to first-price auctions around 2019, and bidders now use bid-shading algorithms for exactly the reasons above.

The highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid. So your bid decides **whether** you win. It does not decide **what you pay**. Bidding your true value v is a weakly dominant strategy (Vickrey, 1961). That means it is never worse than any other bid, whatever the others do:

- **Bidding above v** only changes the outcome when someone else's bid lands between v and your bid. Then you win and pay more than the item is worth to you, so you lose money.
- **Bidding below v** only changes the outcome when the top rival bid lands between your bid and v. Then you lose an item you could have bought at a profit.
- **Bidding exactly v** means you win whenever winning is profitable and lose whenever it isn't.

You don't need to guess anything about the other bidders. All the work is in figuring out your own value honestly.

## First-price sealed bid: shade your bid

The winner pays their own bid. If you bid your true value you make zero profit even when you win, so you have to bid below it. Lowering your bid has a tradeoff:

- You keep more profit when you win: v − b gets bigger.
- You win less often, because someone else is more likely to outbid you.

The best bid balances these two effects. In the standard textbook case (n bidders, risk-neutral, private values drawn independently and uniformly), the equilibrium bid is:

> **b(v) = ((n − 1)/n) × v**

| Bidders (n) | Bid as a share of your value |
|---|---|
| 2 | 50% |
| 3 | 67% |
| 5 | 80% |
| 10 | 90% |

A more general rule: bid what you expect the strongest rival's value to be, assuming yours is the highest. In symbols, b(v) = E[highest other value | it is below v]. In effect, you bid what you would have paid in a second-price auction.

**Example:** The item is worth $100 to you and you face one rival whose value is equally likely to be anywhere from $0 to $100. In a Vickrey auction, bid $100. In a first-price auction, bid about $50. With nine rivals, bid about $90.

## Practical rules for first-price bidding

1. **More competition means less shading.** As the number of bidders grows, bids move toward true values.
2. **Your beliefs about rivals matter.** If you expect strong rivals, shade less. If you expect weak ones, shade more. This is why first-price auctions reward research and strategy, and Vickrey auctions don't.
3. **Risk aversion means bidding higher.** If losing hurts more than overpaying a little, shade less. This matters in first-price auctions only. In a Vickrey auction the best bid is still your true value.
4. **Ties and bid levels:** Avoid round numbers. $50.37 beats someone else's $50.

## Two points that apply to both formats

- **Expected revenue is usually the same.** Under the standard assumptions, the seller expects the same revenue from either format (the revenue equivalence theorem). The lower first-price bids exactly offset the fact that Vickrey winners pay only the second-highest bid. With n uniform bidders, expected revenue is (n−1)/(n+1) in both cases.
- **Winner's curse with common values.** If the item has a shared value that everyone is estimating, such as an oil lease, you should lower your estimate in both formats. Winning means you were probably the most optimistic bidder. "Bid your value" in a Vickrey auction means your value given that you won, not your raw estimate.

## Where the theory breaks down

- **Trust in the seller:** Vickrey truthfulness assumes the seller won't add fake bids (shill bids) to push up the second price. That risk is one reason pure Vickrey auctions are rare in practice.
- **Real-world formats differ:** eBay's proxy bidding works roughly like a second-price auction, so entering your true maximum there is sensible. Many online ad exchanges switched to first-price auctions around 2019, and bidders now use bid-shading algorithms for exactly the reasons above.

answer:
**The Tale of Genji** (*Genji monogatari*) was written by **Murasaki Shikibu**, a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court during the Heian period. She wrote it in the **early 11th century** and probably finished it **around 1010**.

**About the author**
- "Murasaki Shikibu" isn't her real name, which is unknown. It's a court nickname. "Shikibu" probably comes from her father's post in the Ministry of Ceremonial, and "Murasaki" may come from a character in the novel.
- She came from a minor branch of the Fujiwara clan. She served Empress Shōshi (also called Akiko), the consort of Emperor Ichijō.

**When it was written**
- Britannica says she likely finished the novel about 1010, while she was serving at court.
- How long she worked on it is debated. Some critics think she wrote the whole thing between about 1001 and 1005. Britannica considers it more likely that writing such a long and complex work took much longer.
- Other sources give a range of about 1000 to 1012. A diary entry by the author of the *Sarashina Nikki* suggests the tale existed in its present form by 1021.

**Why it matters**
It's generally considered the greatest work of Japanese literature, and it's often called the world's first or oldest full novel.

answer:
The attacker doesn't spend the same coins twice inside one chain, because valid nodes would reject that. What they do is pay you on the chain everyone can see, then swap in a different version of recent history where that payment never happened. Proof-of-work nodes always switch to the valid chain with the most accumulated work. If the attacker has most of the hash power, they can build the heavier chain, so the network accepts their version.

## The rule being exploited

Every node follows one fork-choice rule: among the valid chains it knows about, it treats the one with the most total proof-of-work as the real one. People usually call it "the longest chain." The Bitcoin whitepaper puts it this way: "The majority decision is represented by the longest chain, which has the greatest proof-of-work effort invested in it," and "nodes always consider the longest chain to be the correct one." Its security assumption is that "if a majority of CPU power is controlled by honest nodes, the honest chain will grow the fastest." A 51% attack is what happens when that assumption fails.

## How a double-spend works, step by step

1. **Pay someone publicly.** The attacker sends, say, 1,000 coins to an exchange (transaction A). It goes into a block on the public chain and starts collecting confirmations.
2. **Mine a secret chain at the same time.** Starting from the block just before transaction A, the attacker uses their hash power to build a competing chain that they don't broadcast. In that chain they include a conflicting transaction B, which sends the same 1,000 coins back to a wallet they control. A and B spend the same inputs, so they can never both be valid in one chain.
3. **Collect what they paid for.** The exchange waits for its required number of confirmations, say 6 or 50 blocks, then credits the deposit. The attacker trades the coins for another asset and withdraws it. That withdrawn value is the profit.
4. **Pull ahead.** With more than half the network's hash power, the secret chain grows faster than the honest one on average. Eventually it has more total work, however many blocks behind it started.
5. **Release the secret chain.** The attacker broadcasts it. Every honest node checks it, sees it is valid and heavier, and reorganizes: it drops the honest blocks since the fork point and adopts the attacker's blocks.
6. **The payment disappears.** In the new canonical history, transaction B already spent the coins, so transaction A is now invalid and can't be re-mined. The exchange's deposit no longer exists, but the exchange has already sent out the other asset. The attacker ends up with both the original coins and whatever they bought.

All the honest blocks that were dropped also lose their block rewards, and their other transactions return to the mempool or become invalid if they conflict.

## Why "51%" matters

Confirmations protect you because a minority attacker who starts behind has to catch up. Nakamoto modeled this race as a random walk, like the gambler's ruin problem. If the attacker has less than half the hash power, the chance of ever catching up drops exponentially with each block they're behind. The whitepaper's table shows how many confirmations push an attacker's success chance below 0.1%:

| Attacker's hash share | Confirmations needed |
|---|---|
| 10% | 5 |
| 20% | 11 |
| 30% | 24 |
| 40% | 89 |
| 45% | 340 |

Above 50%, the table stops working. The attacker's chain grows faster on average, so they will catch up with near certainty eventually, no matter how many confirmations you wait for. More confirmations only make the attack longer and more expensive. That's why a majority is the threshold. The number is about 50%, not exactly 51%, and attacks with somewhat less hash power can still succeed against a few confirmations with some luck.

## What a 51% attacker can't do

The whitepaper notes that a successful attack "does not throw the system open to arbitrary changes." The attacker's blocks still have to pass every validity rule, so they can't:

- spend coins from other people's addresses, because they don't have the private keys to sign those transactions;
- create coins out of nothing or give themselves a bigger block reward;
- change the protocol rules.

In the whitepaper's words, the attacker "can only try to change one of his own transactions to take back money he recently spent." They can also censor transactions, meaning keep them out of blocks, and orphan other miners' blocks, but the double-spend is the main way to profit.

## In practice

- **Big chains are mostly protected by cost.** Getting a majority of Bitcoin's hash power would take huge amounts of specialized hardware and electricity. The attack would also likely crash the coin's price, which hurts the attacker's own holdings and the value of their mining equipment.
- **Small chains get hit.** Coins that share a mining algorithm with a bigger network, or whose hash power can be rented, are much cheaper to attack. Ethereum Classic had deep reorganizations with double-spends, including one Coinbase detected in 2019 and two in about a week in 2020. Bitcoin SV had a 2021 attack that reportedly rolled back hundreds of thousands of transactions. The victims were usually exchanges, since they accept large deposits and let people withdraw quickly into other assets.
- **The usual defense** for anyone accepting large payments on a low-hash-power chain is to wait for many more confirmations. Exchanges raised their limits on such chains to hundreds or even thousands of blocks after these attacks. Watching for sudden deep reorganizations helps too.

Nagarjuna (c. 150–250 CE, probably in southern India) founded the Madhyamaka, or "Middle Way," school of Buddhist philosophy. His central claim is that **everything is empty (śūnya) of *svabhāva***. *Svabhāva* is usually translated as "intrinsic nature," "inherent existence" or "own-being." Emptiness does **not** mean that nothing exists. It means that nothing exists independently, on its own terms, with a fixed essence. Things exist only in dependence on other things.

## 1. What is being denied: *svabhāva*
Some earlier Buddhist schools, especially the Abhidharma schools such as the Sarvāstivāda, broke the world down into basic building blocks called *dharmas*. They held that each *dharma* "bears its own nature." Persons and chariots were seen as convenient fictions, but the ultimate constituents were thought to be truly real. Nagarjuna takes the analysis one step further. He argues that even these supposed foundations have no independent essence, so there is no bottom level of reality that exists from its own side.

His main argument is that a thing with real *svabhāva* would have to be:
- **independent**, not produced by causes and conditions,
- **unchanging**, because an essence that could become something else would not be an essence.

Things like that could never arise, change, interact or cease. Yet we see things arising and changing all the time. So whatever arises and changes cannot have *svabhāva*.

## 2. Emptiness = dependent origination
The key verse is *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (MMK, "Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way") 24.18:

> "Whatever is dependently arisen, that is explained to be emptiness. That, being a dependent designation, is itself the middle way."

Emptiness is therefore not a hidden substance or a cosmic void. It is the other side of the Buddha's teaching of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Things depend on other things in several ways:
- **causally**, on causes and conditions,
- **mereologically**, on their parts (a chariot depends on its wheels and axle, and these depend on their own parts, with no end),
- **conceptually**, on the concepts and conventions by which we pick them out ("long" exists only relative to "short").

These chains of dependence never reach a self-standing foundation.

Nagarjuna's method is mostly critical. He takes concepts such as causation, motion, time, the self and even nirvana, and shows case by case that they become incoherent if you assume they refer to things with intrinsic natures. A famous example is his opening treatment of causation (MMK 1.1). If things had *svabhāva*, they could arise from themselves, from something else, from both, or from neither. He argues that each of the four options fails. This four-part structure, the *catuṣkoṭi* or "tetralemma," appears throughout his work.

## 3. The "Middle Way": neither eternalism nor nihilism
The name means a middle path between two extremes:
- **Eternalism (reification):** treating things as solidly, independently real.
- **Nihilism:** concluding that nothing exists at all, or that causes, ethics and the path to liberation don't matter.

Emptiness avoids both. Because things lack fixed essences, they can change, causes can produce effects, and suffering can end. In MMK 24 an opponent objects that emptiness would destroy the Four Noble Truths. Nagarjuna turns the objection around: it is *svabhāva* that would make the Buddhist path impossible. "For whom emptiness is possible, everything is possible" (24.14). A person with a fixed nature could never become enlightened.

## 4. The two truths
Nagarjuna separates two levels of truth (MMK 24.8–10):
- **Conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*):** the everyday world of tables, persons, causes and moral responsibility. It is fully valid within its own terms.
- **Ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*):** that all of these are empty of intrinsic nature.

He insists that "without relying on the conventional, the ultimate cannot be taught, and without understanding the ultimate, nirvana is not attained." Emptiness does not throw away the conventional world. It shows what kind of reality that world has. Many modern interpreters go further. They argue that the ultimate truth is not a deeper hidden reality behind appearances, but simply the fact that there is no such reality. On this reading, conventional truth is in a sense all the truth there is.

A striking consequence is that "there is not the slightest difference between samsara and nirvana" (MMK 25.19–20). Neither has an essence. Nirvana is not an escape to another realm but a different way of relating to this one.

## 5. The emptiness of emptiness
Emptiness is itself empty. It is not an absolute that exists independently. Nagarjuna warns that people who turn emptiness into a view or a metaphysical position are "incurable" (MMK 13.8). He compares misunderstood emptiness to grabbing a snake by the wrong end (24.11). Emptiness works like a medicine that cures attachment to fixed views and then leaves the body along with the illness.

## 6. "I have no thesis"
In the *Vigrahavyāvartanī* ("Dispelling Disputes"), critics from the Nyāya school argued that the claim "all things are empty" defeats itself. If the claim is empty, how can it refute anything? If it is not empty, then not everything is empty. Nagarjuna replied that he advances no thesis claiming to capture an independently real state of affairs, "so the fault is not mine" (v. 29). His words are themselves empty and dependently arisen, but like a conjured illusion they can still do work. Here that work is dispelling a mistaken belief. Scholars still debate exactly how to read this reply.

## 7. Why it matters, the practical point
For Nagarjuna, emptiness is not an abstract puzzle. We instinctively project fixed, independent existence onto ourselves and the things we want or fear. That projection fuels grasping and suffering. Seeing through it changes how things appear to us and loosens that grip. This is why emptiness is presented as a path to liberation, not only as a theory.

## Key works
- *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (about 450 verses), his main work
- *Vigrahavyāvartanī*, replies to his critics
- *Śūnyatāsaptati* ("Seventy Verses on Emptiness")
- *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā* ("Sixty Verses on Reasoning")
- *Ratnāvalī* ("Precious Garland"), which contains ethical advice addressed to a king

His ideas shaped later Indian Madhyamaka thinkers such as Candrakīrti, as well as Tibetan Buddhism and East Asian Buddhism, including the Chan/Zen traditions. A good English translation of the MMK to start with is Jay Garfield's *The Fundamental Wisdom of the Middle Way*, or Mark Siderits and Shōryū Katsura's *Nāgārjuna's Middle Way*.

# Why quantum computers threaten Bitcoin and Ethereum, and what has to change (as of 21 October 2026)

## Short answer

Bitcoin and Ethereum prove who owns coins with elliptic-curve digital signatures. Bitcoin uses ECDSA and Schnorr on the secp256k1 curve, and Ethereum accounts use ECDSA on the same curve. These schemes are safe only because nobody can work out a private key from its public key. A large, error-corrected quantum computer running **Shor's algorithm** could do that, which means it could forge signatures and spend other people's coins.

To fix this, both networks have to switch to **post-quantum signature schemes**, and every user has to move funds to the new kind of address or account. The cryptography already exists. The hard parts are signature size, the coordination and politics of changing the protocol, and deciding what happens to coins whose owners never move them.

**No such machine exists today.** The threat is in the future, but the estimated hardware needed has dropped sharply.

## 1. What a quantum computer actually breaks

**Signatures (the serious problem).** Shor's algorithm solves the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem efficiently. In March 2026, Google Quantum AI, working with researchers from the Ethereum Foundation and Stanford, published estimates for breaking 256-bit elliptic-curve crypto on secp256k1:
- one circuit needs fewer than 1,200 logical qubits and about 90 million Toffoli gates;
- another needs fewer than 1,450 logical qubits and about 70 million Toffoli gates;
- on a superconducting machine, that works out to **fewer than 500,000 physical qubits**, roughly 20 times fewer than earlier estimates, and could run "in a few minutes."

Google withheld the actual circuits and published a zero-knowledge proof so others can check the claim. It recommended that blockchains move to post-quantum cryptography, that users stop reusing exposed addresses, and that communities decide on a policy for abandoned coins.

For scale, publicly known machines in mid-2026 reportedly had a few thousand noisy physical qubits and were not fault-tolerant at the scale required. That figure comes from secondary reporting.

**Hashing and mining (a minor problem).** Grover's algorithm only gives a square-root speedup against hash functions like SHA-256 and Keccak. It is widely considered impractical as a way to dominate mining. It also doesn't seriously weaken the hashes that hide public keys behind addresses.

## 2. Why "public key exposure" matters

An attacker needs your **public key**, not just your address. When that key becomes visible determines the type of attack.

- **Long-exposure ("at rest") attacks.** The public key is already on-chain, so an attacker has unlimited time to work on it. In Bitcoin this covers:
  - early pay-to-public-key (P2PK) outputs, including roughly 1.1 million BTC attributed to Satoshi;
  - reused addresses, where spending once revealed the key;
  - Taproot outputs, whose key-path design puts a tweaked public key directly in the output.

  Estimates of exposed BTC range from about **6 to 6.9 million BTC, roughly 30–34% of supply**. Glassnode put it at about 6.26 million BTC (31.2%) in October 2026. Google's paper estimated about 6.7 million, of which around 2.3 million are also dormant.
- **Short-exposure ("in transit") attacks.** When you spend from an unexposed address, your public key appears in the mempool before the transaction is confirmed. A fast enough quantum computer could derive your key and broadcast a competing transaction that pays the attacker. Bitcoin's roughly 10-minute block time makes the "minutes" runtime estimates worrying.
- **Ethereum** has the same weakness. Once an account sends any transaction, its public key can be recovered from the signature. Since nearly every active account has sent something, nearly every active account is exposed. Accounts that have only received ETH show only an address, which gives some protection.

**Ethereum has more exposed components than Bitcoin.** Its official roadmap lists:
- ECDSA account signatures;
- BLS signatures that validators use for consensus;
- KZG commitments used for rollup data availability;
- pairing-based SNARK proof systems.

Bitcoin's main problem is user signatures. Ethereum's proof-of-stake consensus layer also relies on elliptic-curve cryptography.

## 3. What Bitcoin would have to change

1. **New quantum-resistant output types.** BIP-360, "Pay-to-Merkle-Root" (P2MR), was merged into the BIP repository in February 2026 and is still a **Draft**; the latest version is v0.12.1 from July 2026. It works like Taproot without the key-path spend, so the public key isn't sitting in the output. Addresses would start with `bc1z`. It protects against long-exposure attacks only. It does **not** add post-quantum signatures, which would need a separate proposal, and it does not stop mempool attacks on its own. It has not activated on mainnet, and coverage reports no implementation work in Bitcoin Core yet.
2. **Post-quantum signature opcodes.** This would mean adding schemes such as NIST's lattice-based ML-DSA (Dilithium) or FN-DSA (Falcon), or hash-based SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+). The cost is size. Post-quantum signatures are usually kilobytes, compared with about 64 bytes today, so fees rise and fewer transactions fit in a block.
3. **Mass migration.** Every holder has to move coins to the new outputs. With Bitcoin's limited block space, moving tens of millions of UTXOs could take months or longer.
4. **Deciding what to do with coins that never move.** This is the most contested question. BIP-361, from Jameson Lopp and co-authors, is a draft that has not been activated. It proposes:
   - **Phase A:** ban sending funds to quantum-vulnerable address types;
   - **Phase B:** about five years after activation, restrict old ECDSA/Schnorr spends behind a quantum-safe rescue protocol, which in effect freezes coins that haven't migrated.

   Supporters say this stops a quantum attacker from taking Satoshi's coins and dumping them on the market. Critics say it amounts to confiscation and breaks Bitcoin's "your keys, your coins" principle. Either way, it would need a soft fork, and Bitcoin's process for that is slow and conservative.

## 4. What Ethereum would have to change

As of its September 2026 update, ethereum.org's roadmap includes:

- **Consensus:** replace BLS validator signatures with **leanXMSS**, a hash-based scheme. Those signatures are much larger, so they would be aggregated and compressed (about 250×) using STARK proofs via "leanVM." Multiple client teams are already running post-quantum consensus devnets.
- **Data availability:** replace KZG commitments with STARK-based or lattice-based alternatives. Both are still being researched for practicality at scale.
- **User accounts:** use account abstraction to give "signature agility," so individual accounts can switch to post-quantum signatures early. The relevant proposal is EIP-8141, under consideration for the Hegotá upgrade in the second half of 2026. Later planning milestones include a post-quantum key registry, native post-quantum signature verification and full post-quantum aggregation. These milestones are not commitments.
- **Timeline:** the Ethereum Foundation formed a dedicated Post-Quantum team in January 2026. It targets **around 2029** for core post-quantum infrastructure, with full migration of the execution layer and wider ecosystem taking longer. Critics have questioned whether that timeline is realistic.

Ethereum has two practical advantages: regular hard forks and smart-contract wallets. Both make it easier to change signature schemes than in Bitcoin. In exchange, it has more cryptographic pieces to replace.

## 5. Why this matters now if the machine doesn't exist

- **Migration takes years.** It means protocol changes, wallet and exchange upgrades, hardware-wallet support and users actually moving funds. NIST plans to deprecate ECDSA by 2030 and disallow it by 2035, and Google has set its own post-quantum migration target for 2029.
- **Coins exposed now stay exposed.** A public key already on-chain can be attacked whenever a capable machine appears, so waiting doesn't help those coins.
- **Estimates keep falling.** The March 2026 paper cut the requirement by about 20×, and later papers (for example from Caltech/Oratomic and Georgia Tech) suggested other routes. Nobody can give a reliable date, but the safety margin is shrinking.

## What you can do today

- **Don't reuse addresses.** Use a fresh address for each receipt so your public key stays hidden until you spend.
- **Keep wallet software updated** so you can migrate when quantum-safe address types go live.
- **Follow your exchange's or custodian's plans,** since they hold a large share of exposed coins (about 1.66 million BTC by one analysis).
- **Be skeptical of "quantum-proof coin" marketing.** Many sources in this area are promotional.

answer:
Dostoevsky never gives Raskolnikov one clear reason for killing the pawnbroker Alyona Ivanovna, and that is deliberate. Raskolnikov tells himself several reasons, and the novel slowly shows that the noble-sounding ones were mostly covers. By the end, his deepest motive is that he wanted to prove to himself that he was an "extraordinary" man who had the right to step over moral law.

**1. Poverty and family pressure (the practical reason)**
He is a former student who had to drop out, and he lives starving in a tiny garret in St. Petersburg. A letter from his mother tells him that his sister Dunya plans to marry Luzhin, a smug man she doesn't love, largely to help Rodion. He finds this sacrifice unbearable and wants a way to stop needing it. The pawnbroker's money seems to offer one.

**2. The utilitarian argument ("one death, a hundred lives")**
In a tavern he overhears a student telling an officer that killing the old woman would be justified. She is a greedy "louse" who exploits the poor, and her money could pay for a thousand good deeds. These are the same thoughts Raskolnikov has already been having. He tells himself the murder would be a net gain for society and that he would use the money to start a useful life and help others.

**3. The "extraordinary man" theory (the core motive)**
Months earlier he had published an article, "On Crime," which the detective Porfiry Petrovich later questions him about. It splits humanity into two groups:
- **"Ordinary" people**, who must obey the law and exist mainly to reproduce.
- **"Extraordinary" people**, like Napoleon, who have an inner right to "step over" laws, even over blood, if their idea requires it.

The murder becomes a test of which group he belongs to. When he finally confesses to Sonya, he drops the charitable excuses. He says he wanted to become a Napoleon, and that he killed "for myself, for myself alone." He wanted to find out whether he was a "trembling creature" or someone who "has the right," a louse like everyone else or a real man. He also says, "I didn't kill a human being, I killed a principle."

**4. Chance and compulsion**
Dostoevsky also gives the crime an almost fated quality. Raskolnikov happens to overhear in the Haymarket that Lizaveta, the pawnbroker's half-sister, will be out at a certain hour the next evening. After that he acts in a feverish, half-willing state, as if carried along by events.

**How the novel judges his reasons**
The theory falls apart almost immediately. He also kills Lizaveta, a meek and innocent woman, which destroys his idea that he killed only a "louse" or a "principle." He barely uses the stolen money; he hides it under a stone without even counting it. Instead of feeling strong, he falls into fever, paranoia, and isolation. His own suffering shows him that he is not a Napoleon. Critics still argue about how sincere his altruism ever was. Many read it as a rationalization for a wish for power or self-proof. The book's answer is that the real motive was pride, and that the punishment is psychological long before it is legal.

**In short:** He tells himself he kills for money and for the good of humanity. In truth he kills to test a theory that he is above ordinary morality, and the rest of the novel shows that theory collapsing.
